doc.title: Charles McPherson interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Lonnie Hillyer, his friend and fellow Detroiter
summary: Hillyer lived on his street, was talented but unrecognized, and died in 1985.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: The name Lonnie Hillyer comes up.

Yeah. Lonnie lived right on my street. He’s about almost a year younger. He died in 1985. Very, very talented. Very, you know he’s one of these guys that you always read about, you always read about this prototype talented person, died young, no one knew who in the heck he was. I mean there are of course — some musicians know. But he never got any recognition, he never was involved in any real say visible records. He did

make a record with Yusef Lateef, he might have been involved with James Moody on a record or something like that, but he never, he was kind of a tragic figure. He never just got his just due and he wasn’t around long enough. And then, it’s kind of sad. But anyway he was my best friend. Very talented. Very, very talented. And he just died in 1985, a young man. He was about 45. It was just one of those things. We went to New York together, as far as working with Mingus, yes. Yeah, we worked, let’s see this was around 1959 or ‘60. And there used to be a little coffee shop in the Village called the Cafe Wha?. And there were people I can remember folk singing was very popular at this time, as well as the jazz. And quite often they would have folk singing and jazz in the same club. In fact there’s a guy, Peter, Paul and Mary, there was a guy named Noel Stookey — he actually changed his name, he was either Peter or Paul.
